subject: 1900 East at Clayton School
comment: Dan, I am not in your district but my son attends Clayton Middle school on 1900 East. I drive him to and from school most days. I have to voice my complaint about the speed bumps currently under construction for the last couple of weeks. First, the timing of construction can't be worse. It causes such a bottleneck around the school during drop off and pickup with the street closed to one lane. This is especially a problem during cold weather when parents are more likely to drive rather than have their kid bike or walk to school. Second, the speed bump virus going around Salt Lake is unbearable. I no longer shop at Emigration market or Jolley's pharmacy because of the annoyance of driving over so many speed bumps to get to those places. I look forward to the day we have an administration in the city that will take a bulldozer to them. 1900 East has been a great street for 100 years. It is the route I could safely take as a kid riding my bike from the U to my grandparents house just north of the freeway on 20th East. If anything, I can't believe how bad the asphalt is on the street and why it hasn't been repaired in years. Speed bumps are not what that street needs. Please step up and make better plans for your neighborhood. Ben Fonnesbeck

subject: Concerns Regarding ICE Detention Facilities in Salt Lake City
comment: Subject: Concerns Regarding ICE Detention Facilities in Salt Lake City To the Members of the Salt Lake City Council, I am writing to urge the Council to consider and pass an emergency ordinance requiring a conditional use permit for ICE detention facilities in Salt Lake City. Such a measure would provide the City Council and Planning Commission with the legal authority to prevent the construction and operation of detention facilities that pose serious ethical, legal, and humanitarian concerns. ICE detention facilities have a well-documented history of inhumane conditions, including failures to provide adequate food, medical care, and basic protections for those detained. Reports have shown that ICE has at times stopped paying for detainee medical care even as detention populations increased, placing lives at risk. More recently, ICE has begun detaining children in these facilities, escalating these concerns into clear human rights violations through the neglect and mistreatment of both children and adults. There are also deeply troubling cases in which U.S. citizens—including children—have been detained and transported out of state, separating them from their families, communities, and access to legal counsel. Salt Lake City has a responsibility to protect its residents and uphold fundamental human rights. Allowing the expansion or operation of ICE detention facilities within city limits runs counter to those values and exposes the community to unnecessary harm and liability. I urge the Council to take decisive action to prevent these facilities from operating in Salt Lake City and to stand firmly in defense of human dignity, due process, and community safety. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sincerely, Emma Baker Bountiful, UT

subject: Keep the MU-8 Zoning east of St. Marks Cathedral
comment: The City Council should keep the current MU-8 zoning for the property at 265 East 100 South for three reasons. First, the proposal to change the property to D-1 to accommodate the developer's quest to build a higher building than the MU-8 zoning allows goes against the long-term City policy of having firm boundaries define the downtown. The City's plans consistently have set the downtown's eastern boundary at roughly 250 East Street to keep the downtown from bleeding eastward into residential areas. A 1988 Regional/Urban Design Assistance Team study advised the City to "develop a new 'Urban Neighborhood" zoning classification for the area bounded by a mid-block line between 200 East and 300 East to provide for "urban neighborhoods" to envelop the commercial core and make the downtown the focal point of high-quality, high-density development and design. It's the reason the downtown is what it is today. It is the result of the study's advice that, "the community will only succeed in redeveloping downtown if the major stakeholders (including the City, LDS Church, developers, and the business community, and neighborhoods) can support a single vision and strategy for downtown and pursue it consistently over a period of time." Second, the MU-8 zoning has not had enough time for the City to see whether the zoning will work. The Council adopted the zoning in 2025. Why not see what the zoning will accomplish instead of immediately responding to a developer's pleading of special case? The developer must have known what the City's plans were to implement the MU-8 zone. Why seek to change it? The City Council staff report raises a similar issue. According to the report, "It is important to note that if the zoning map amendment is adopted by the Council there is no guarantee the proposed development will be constructed. The property could be redeveloped with any use allowed within the zone or sold to another party. The Council is only being asked to consider rezoning the property. Because zoning of a property can outlast the life of a building, any rezoning application should be considered on the merits of changing the zoning of that property, not simply based on a potential project." (Staff Report, Page 3.) The City faced a similar issue with the proposed residential building at the corner of 1100 East and 2100 South and stayed with the existing zoning. Sugar House is going to get a much, much better building that fits into the fabric of that area because of the City's decision to adhere to existing plans. Third, the Sugar House residential building and the earlier proposal to build a gas station and convenience store by Sugar House Park raise another point. Do the proposed buildings, even if the main structure is capped at 225 feet, fit into the neighborhood? Except for the law offices at the corner of 200 East 100 South, the buildings along 100 South are low-key condominiums and apartment buildings sharing space with neighborhood businesses - and St. Marks Cathedral. Is that a neighborhood that warrants an edifice? Like the original building proposed in Sugar House, the proposed building in the proposed D-1 zone is an underwhelming design that will overwhelm the existing neighborhood. The design for the building that complies with the MU-8 zoning shown in the transmittal and staff report portrays a better structure that fits into the neighborhood.

subject: Inquiry regarding Call 2 Haul eligibility and policy equity
comment: Dear SLC Sustainability Department and City Council Members, I am writing to request a policy update to the Call 2 Haul program that would extend eligibility to residents in multi-family buildings. I am a homeowner at REDACTED. Our building houses 48 families on a footprint equivalent to roughly six suburban lots. Despite this being the exact model of "smart growth" the city promotes, we are currently excluded from the Call 2 Haul program due to its restriction to properties with 1–4 units. I have bulk items ready for disposal and would prefer to utilize a city-sanctioned program. I am seeking either a policy update to include multi-family properties or guidance on a service buy-in option for homeowners in buildings like mine. I understand this limitation may stem from legacy zoning classifications, but I believe it creates an unintended disparity that runs counter to the city's sustainability goals. Residents in Downtown, Central City, Sugar House, and the Granary District amongst many other areas are choosing high-density living to reduce their environmental footprint. However, current eligibility rules inadvertently penalize this choice by denying us access to the diversion services our property taxes help fund. Expanding the program to include multi-family buildings would be consistent with the city's goals for three reasons: Logistical Efficiency: Our building has a centralized dumpster and loading zone. Servicing 48 households at one stop is objectively more carbon-efficient than a city truck traveling to 48 separate suburban driveways. Sustainability Logic: Forcing high-density residents—many of whom do not own large vehicles—to hire private, landfill-bound haulers contradicts the city's goals of reducing emissions and preventing illegal dumping in urban areas. Fiscal Equity: High-density developments contribute significantly more property tax per acre to the General Fund than single-family neighborhoods. We should have equitable access to municipal services, regardless of outdated billing classifications. Could you please direct me to the individual responsible for Call 2 Haul eligibility policy? I would also appreciate understanding the timeline for reviewing these boundaries to better serve the city's growing high-density neighborhoods. Thank you for your time and consideration. Best regards, Justin Justin Kani

subject: Please Support Pro-Housing Policies and the 265 E. 100 South Project
comment: Dear Salt Lake City Council Members, I'm writing as a Salt Lake City resident to encourage you to support pro-housing policies across the city, including the proposed 420-unit residential tower at 265 E. 100 South. I understand there are concerns about the project's impact on a neighboring church's solar panels. I hope the council and developer can find a common-sense solution to address that, but housing for 420 families should be the priority. We need more homes in our downtown core. I've benefited personally from new housing supply, I recently got a great deal on a new apartment. I'd like to buy a home soon too, and that's only possible if we keep building. Thank you for your work on this critical issue. Edgar T. Thornton IV, Salt Lake City

subject: Concerns Regarding ICE Facilities in SLC
comment: To the Salt Lake City Council, I am writing to urge the Council to adopt an emergency ordinance requiring a conditional use permit for any ICE detention facility within Salt Lake City. Doing so would provide the Council and the Planning Commission with the legal authority to prevent the construction and operation of detention facilities that pose serious humanitarian and public safety concerns. ICE detention facilities have a well-documented record of abuse and neglect, including failures to provide adequate medical care, nutrition, and basic human dignity to those in custody. These are not isolated incidents, but systemic problems that have been repeatedly documented by journalists and watchdog organizations. When the state knowingly allows such facilities to operate, it becomes complicit in that harm. The situation becomes even more alarming given that ICE has begun detaining children in these facilities. The detention of children under conditions marked by neglect and trauma constitutes a grave human rights violation. Additionally, these facilities enable U.S. citizens—including children—to be transported out of state, separated from their communities, families, and legal representation. That should concern every resident of this city, regardless of political affiliation. Salt Lake City has long positioned itself as a place that values human dignity, due process, and the safety of its residents. The City Council has both the authority and the responsibility to act when federal practices threaten those values within city limits. Requiring a conditional use permit is a necessary and reasonable step to protect our community from becoming a site of documented abuse and injustice. I urge you to take swift action and pass this emergency ordinance. Thank you for your time and for your service to our city. Sincerely, Kaitlyn Rowbotham Sandy, 84092

subject: Winter water rates and water conservation - D2
comment: Hello, Alejandro, Like everyone, we are very concerned about water conservation. Our SLC policy of basing summer water rates on winter consumption is generally a good policy. However, with the lack of snow, our trees are suffering and require winter water, and trees take a lot! I don't want my trees to die. They are critical to keeping our environment cool in the rising temperatures. It is urgent that you address winter water use and its relationship to summer water rates. I have already decided not to grow a garden next summer because of the high cost of water. This garden feeds not only my family, but is shared with elderly neighbors. As well, I will cut out one third of my grass next summer, but it will entail moving inground sprinkler lines to get water to the apple tree. More expense to save a tree. I have already stopped watering large shrubs at the back portion of our .25 acre lot. I have removed several large shrubs and trees to reduce water. We removed park strip grass in favor of rock and drip lines to 50% green plants. We have learned that we need more water to the old ash tree, which the city will not remove. The city planted a new oak tree in the park strip, which I cannot easily water in the winter. Please, I ask you to address this water crisis by setting a standard water rate across seasons so that I can water my trees this winter without risking higher rates in the summer. Thank you, Deborah Esquibel Hunt

subject: ICE Out Protest
comment: Hello Council Member Dugan, My name is Max, and I am currently a senior at Judge Memorial Catholic High School. I will be graduating in May and moving into the University of Utah dorms this August to begin a four-year degree. My purpose in writing today is to reach out to local leaders about concerns I believe affect people across political lines. There are two main issues I would like to focus on: ICE and political representation. I am fully aware that ICE has been responsible for the deaths of dozens of non-citizens and, more recently, two American citizens in Minneapolis. I do not want to see a situation like this reach Utah. I firmly believe that violence should never be tolerated, let alone excused. At the same time, I do not believe ICE should be abolished. In concept, ICE serves an important purpose and can be useful. My concern is with how it is currently being used — often functioning as a policing force that must follow federal directives while facing very few consequences. Because of this, I believe ICE should be relocated back to the border and refocused on border protection rather than interior enforcement. My second concern relates to political representation, which I believe plays a major role in how issues like this become so polarized. As humans, we naturally label things to better understand them, but political labeling has gone too far. We often agree on nearly everything except one issue, yet that single disagreement can make cooperation feel impossible. I believe people should be able to vote for who they genuinely support, rather than feeling pressured to choose between the two major parties. To help explain this concern, I would like to compare two elections: 1912 and 2012. Both resulted in Democratic victories, but the range of political choice available to voters differed greatly. In 1912, the Progressive Party received 27% of the vote, placing second, while Republicans received 23%. Although Democrats won decisively in the Electoral College with 435 votes, those numbers do not fully reflect voter support across parties. When comparing electoral votes to popular votes, Democrats in 1912 received roughly one electoral vote per 14,540 popular votes, while the Progressive Party received one per 46,800. Even when applying the same comparison to the 2012 election approximately 1:198,000 and 1:296,000 a noticeable imbalance still exists. The Electoral College often encourages campaigns to focus on winning individual states rather than representing the country as a whole. While it was originally intended to balance the power of less populous states with more populous ones, assigning electoral votes largely based on population can have the opposite effect. Instead of creating fairness, it can amplify disparities and shift attention away from broader national electorate. I am not writing to promote one party or ideology over another. Rather, I hope to better understand how local leaders view these issues and whether there is room for policies that encourage accountability, cooperation, and broader representation. I appreciate you taking the time to read this and consider the perspective of a young voter who wants to stay engaged in our community. Sincerely, Max This email reflects my own views and was written by me, with some assistance from AI to improve organization and clarity, for I am not a great writer but a great thinker.
